idiom_name: interface plus implementing classes, wired through a factory or ServiceLoader
implementation_notes: A Java interface already provides the interchangeable-implementation dispatch, so the envelope is usually the interface type itself and no wrapper type is written; a separate facade class is justified when the factory must be hidden, when a narrower API than the implementation's is published, or when a final class with a private final implementation field gives the value-like facade the rest of the program expects. When implementations are discovered instead of constructed, java.util.ServiceLoader (plus a uses/provides declaration in the module descriptor) replaces the hand-written registry. The C++ original's compile-dependency and copy-semantics motivations have no Java analogue: there are no headers, and objects have reference semantics.
pitfalls: Java copies references, so a duplicated envelope shares one mutable letter; the value-like facade is only honest if letters are immutable or copied explicitly.
Adding a method to an interface breaks every implementor unless it is a default method, and a default method quietly gives old implementations behaviour they never wrote.
ServiceLoader instantiates providers lazily and caches them, so provider state persists across call sites; a fresh implementation per use requires an explicit factory instead.
